backformation
A film that seems to be about heritable Monstrous Bitchery in the female line winds up loudly confirming that Monstrous Bitchery—however autonomous it may seem—is a backformation of Patriarchy.
emergent property

Ari Aster, you are something else, and I salute you for your aesthetic commitment to reminding us all that, at its core, Monstrous Bitchery is best understood as an emergent property of Patriarchy itself.
Lamashtean

In this film, the Monstrous Bitch paradigm turns back to its most Lamashtean and Lamian roots: Lamashtu and Lamia are the ultimate evil, false mothers, sacrificing children rather than loving them and caring for them.
decrepitude
Through the increasing decrepitude of Elisabeth’s body, The Substance offers up a staunch critique of the practice of forever pursuing youth, at the expense of being one’s own true, authentic self.
chimeric

This monster, whom the film names Elisasue, is truly, deeply revolting, in large part because she is composite—made of many, many different Elisabeths, all smashed together in a disgusting chimeric body.
subordination

First, Ellen, we find out late in the film, was consecrated and married to Paimon in a ceremony shortly before her death; she wasn’t an autonomous matriarchal monster but a willing and ecstatic participant in her own subordination to Paimon.
talisman

We have forgotten so much, and yet we all know Lamia nonetheless, because the idea of her is everywhere, and has been everywhere since people wrote on clay tablets or talismans, in abject terror that Lamashtu might untimely rip their baby from their womb.
archetype

Because there was a time, long, long ago, before the Monstrous Bitch had come to dominate the patriarchal depiction of powerful women, when the Patriarchy’s stranglehold on Western culture was less, well, strangulating—a time not long after writing had been invented, when the Monstrous Bitch was in circulation along with another powerful female archetype.
hyperinvolved
Annie’s mother, Ellen, was apparently hyperinvolved in Annie’s reproductive life.
corporeal
At any one time, one of the selves has her intact consciousness, and the other self is a corporeal shell, paralyzed on the bathroom floor and receiving intravenous nutrition.
ambivalent

The collapse of the film’s central critique shouldn’t be surprising to us, though, because if there’s one thing we should have learned about depictions of female monstrosity by now, it’s this: Such depictions under Patriarchy are almost always ambivalent.
monstrosity
Seduction, reproductive tampering, spellcasting: the same monstrosity we’ve seen for thousands of years, clawing its rapacious way into the present.
succubus

Eventually, the succubus-like Sue slaughters the crone-like Elisabeth, though without realizing that she—young, gorgeous Sue—will quickly start decaying too, because her fate coincides with Elisabeth’s.
self-mutilation

theological

occult
It’s referring to how both Ellen and Annie herself inherit a larger system of violence, mental illness, trauma, and the occult, by dint of their femaleness.
backslide

Correlatively, public discourse around women’s rights in general appears to be in a nearly vertical backslide: American politicians are unironically suggesting that women’s proper place is in the home—and only in the home.
womb
Annie confesses—in one of the film’s most agonizing scenes—to Peter himself that she repeatedly tried to kill him in the womb, but she failed.
priestess

Annie fulfills the traditional invective-hurling, oath-swearing, curse-casting role of the Monstrous Bitch that goes back to Mesopotamia, cycles through Greece, roils through Rome, and carries through the medieval and early modern period.
